# Nebius raises GPU prices again October 1; H100 to $4.50, B300 to $9.50

Nebius lists higher on demand GPU prices effective October 1, 2026. H100 rises from $3.85 to $4.50 per GPU hour. H200 rises from $4.50 to $5.40, B200 from $7.15 to $8.50, and B300 from $7.85 to $9.50. This round is 17% to 21%. It is reported to be the second increase since May. [1] [2]

Published September 28, 2026 Announced, effective October 1, 2026

## Disclosed terms

HGX H100, per GPU hour

$3.85 now, $4.50 from October 1 [1]

HGX H200, per GPU hour

$4.50 now, $5.40 from October 1 [1]

HGX B200, per GPU hour

$7.15 now, $8.50 from October 1 [1]

HGX B300, per GPU hour

$7.85 now, $9.50 from October 1 [1]

## The disclosure and our analysis

### What changed

Nebius's pricing page now shows two on demand columns: today's rate and a rate effective October 1, 2026. H100 rises 17%, H200 20%, B200 19% and B300 21%. [1]

Spot rates still start at $0.79 for H100 and H200 and $0.99 for B200 and B300. RTX PRO 6000 stays at $1.80. CPU only instances also rise. Nebius still advertises commitment discounts of up to 35% off on demand for multi month cluster reservations. [1]

Nebius's pricing page does not give a reason for the change.

### The second increase this year

This is not the first increase. The Motley Fool reports that in early May, Nebius's pricing page showed H100 at $2.95 per hour and B300 at $6.10. [2] Our own catalog recorded H100 at $3.85 on September 18 and B300 at $7.85 on September 24.

If the May figures are right, the October rates are about 53% higher for H100 and 56% higher for B300 than five months earlier. [2] The trend matters more than any single rate. A budget built on spring pricing may already be out of date.

...

We compared the new rates with published on demand rates in our provider catalog, checked September 18 to 28.

H100: At $4.50, Nebius moves above Runpod ($3.49), Crusoe ($3.90) and Lambda ($4.29). It stays below CoreWeave's 8 GPU instance, about $6.16 per GPU.

H200: At $5.40, Nebius moves above Runpod ($4.59) and Verda ($4.55). It stays below Together AI ($5.99) and CoreWeave (about $6.31 per GPU).

B200: At $8.50, Nebius moves well above Lambda ($6.69) and Runpod ($6.79). CoreWeave's 8 GPU instance works out to about $8.60 per GPU.

B300: At $9.50, Nebius moves above Verda ($8.20) and Scaleway ($7.50). Together AI lists $9.99.

Configurations differ. vCPUs, memory, storage, networking and minimum allocation all vary. A lower hourly rate is not a lower project cost on its own.

### What to do before October 1

Ask about locking today's rate. Ask Nebius whether a commitment signed before October 1 is priced at the current rate. Get the answer in writing, with the rate and term.

If you run on Nebius on demand today, your bill goes up October 1 unless your contract says otherwise. Check whether your agreement fixes the rate.

If you have a Nebius quote in hand, ask which rate it uses. A quote issued in September may still show the old price.

If you are planning a project, get a dated quote for your actual start date. Ask what a 3, 6 or 12 month commitment costs against the new on demand rate. Ask whether that commitment reserves GPUs or only lowers the rate.

- Pricing is still rising... 5yr market rate is now ~$19bn per GW-year (and is our GOOGL base case), short-term capacity clears at ~$40bn with two witnesses, and NBIS lifts list prices 17-21% from Oct 1st

- Supply got tighter again... Oracle’s New Mexico Stargate campus now carries a force majeure notice and a reported one-year slip, and Texas has frozen data-center permits pending a grid audit
- Thesis intact - owns integration and NBIS…

- The market five-year rate now sits on our base case... SemiAnalysis puts five-year GB300 contracts at $4.50 to 4.60 per GPU-hour, about $19bn per GW-year, against our $18bn base case for uncontracted capacity
- Short-term pricing has two new marks… CoreWeave’s 3-6 month contracts at ~$40bn per GW-year (Sep 17) match Nebius’s short-term tier of $40-50bn
- Top of the market is SpaceX... Anthropic pays $1.25bn a month for Colossus 1, roughly $45 to 50bn per GW-year on 300MW+… that is immediacy pricing on sunk capex, with a 90-day termination right after December

highlights:
# Chmura AI drożeje 

 Nebius poinformował klientów o podniesieniu stawek za wynajem mocy obliczeniowej GPU od 1 października. 

 Publikacja: 28.09.2026 06:00 

 Konrad Ogrodowicz, zarządzający funduszami, Superfund TFI 

 Foto: materiały prasowe 

 Konrad Ogrodowicz 

 To już druga podwyżka w ciągu trzech miesięcy. Instancje z chipami Nvidia H100 zdrożeją o ok. 17 proc., H200 o 20 proc., B200 o ok. 19 proc., a najnowsze B300 najmocniej, bo o 21 proc. Stawka za godzinę pracy H100 wzrośnie z 3,85 do 4,50 USD, a za H200 z 4,50 do 5,40 USD. Drożeją także CPU i pamięć. Stawki za część usług opartych na procesorach AMD EPYC Genoa rosną o ok. 25 proc., a za pamięć o ok. 41 proc., co jest największą podwyżką w nowym cenniku. 

 Wielu inwestorów obawia się, że zbliżamy się do szczytu cyklu AI, a tym samym do szczytu notowań spółek technologicznych. Na razie ta teza nie znajduje jednak potwierdzenia w danych napływających z rynku. Popyt na moc obliczeniową jest tak duży, że każda nowa moc jest w pełni wykorzystywana. Do tego branża napotyka kolejne wąskie gardła, które spowalniają inwestycje. Ostatnio głośno było o problemach z przyłączami energetycznymi w Teksasie, gdzie kolejka oczekujących na podłączenie do sieci jest zbyt długa. 

 Inwestorzy przyjęli podwyżki pozytywnie, a akcje Nebiusa zyskały ok. 8 proc. W mojej ocenie neochmury to jedna z ciekawszych inwestycji na najbliższy rok. Czołówkę tego sektora tworzą Nebius, CoreWeave i IREN. Oczekiwania inwestorów są wysokie, ale, jak widać, wciąż jest sporo miejsca na pozytywne zaskoczenia. Spółki te są dopiero na początku drogi, a jednocześnie dysponują potężnym portfelem zamówień, którego rynek, moim zdaniem, jeszcze w pełni nie wycenił.

results.title: Nebius will raise hourly GPU prices by up to 21% on Oct. 1 · Infive
highlights:
Nebius will raise on-demand rates for four Nvidia GPU models by 17% to 21% on Oct. 1, including B300 from $7.85 to $9.50 an hour. CFO Dado Alonso said in August that capacity sold out as fast as it came online; existing contracts won't be repriced.

The increases cover H100, H200, B200 and B300 GPUs, plus CPU-only servers. Nebius listed the H100 at $2.95 an hour and the B300 at $6.10 in early May; after the new rates, they will cost $4.50 and $9.50—about 53% and 56% more, respectively.

Nebius does not disclose how much revenue comes from hourly rentals versus reserved-capacity contracts. At June's end, it reported $37.5 billion in remaining performance obligations—signed revenue not yet recognized—more than 60 times its $582 million second-quarter revenue. The Oct. 1 increase won't reprice that backlog and mainly signals rates for capacity not yet sold; the article warns prices could fall if supply catches up.

results.title: Computing power futures near launch, B200 price market sees 87% increase in two weeks. - BlockBeats
highlights: According to monitoring by PolyBeats, on the prediction market Polymarket, the probability of "the Ornn B200 index reaching $7.50 this month" has risen from a low of 5.7% two weeks ago to 93%, an increase of 87.3 percentage points. Ornn data shows that its B200 index rose from $7.19/GPU hour on September 14 to $8.08/GPU hour on September 27, an increase of about 12.4% over two weeks. The B200 index refers to the compute rental price index for Nvidia's Blackwell architecture B200 GPU, measuring how much it costs to rent one B200 for 1 hour, in units of $/GPU hour. Nebius's pricing page shows that its HGX B200 on-demand price will increase from $7.15/GPU hour to $8.50/GPU hour starting October 1, a rise of about 18.9%; prices for H100, H200, and B300 will also be raised accordingly. Compute itself is shifting from cloud services to a tradable commodity. ICE and Ornn have announced plans to launch cash-settled GPU compute futures based on the Ornn index, with coverage potentially including H100, H200, and B200; CME plans to launch H100 and B200 compute futures on October 5, still subject to regulatory review. In the future, AI companies will be able to lock in compute costs in advance just as airlines hedge oil prices, and compute prices will also develop clearer spot, forward, and hedging markets.

results.title: Nebius's Oct. 1 Price Hike: The 41% Memory Jump Is the Real Signal | AInvest
highlights:
A cloud company raising prices usually reads as margin-grabbing. When AI-cloud provider Nebius NBIS-- (NBIS) told customers on Sept. 17 that pay-as-you-go rates on its Nvidia NVDA-- GPUs would climb 17% to 21% starting Oct. 1, the stock rose on the news rather than fell. The market smelled scarcity, not greed, and that is the right read - but only half of it. The line in the notice that says the most is the roughly 41% increase on memory, and understanding why memory went up twice as fast as the chips tells you where this AI compute cycle is actually binding.

Start with what a price hike means in a cloud business. Renting out Nvidia chips is a supply-constrained game: when demand outstrips the fleet a provider can stand up, the scarce few raise list prices - the same fingerprint as the 2023 H100 shortage. Nebius made its on-demand rates 17% to 21% higher on selected GPUs, raised some CPU-only instances by 25%, and lifted memory about 41%. It was the company's second price rise in a matter of months, and it is not a Nebius quirk: competitor CoreWeave reportedly signed contracts at higher prices the same day. When the whole rental market reprices up together, that is demand, not one operator testing its pricing power.

Now the detail that carries the story. The percentages are not uniform because the scarcity is not uniform. Per GPU-hour, the H100 went from $3.85 to $4.50 and the H200 from $4.50 to $5.40, while the newest Blackwell parts rose the most - the B200 to $8.50 and the B300 to $9.50. Memory was the outlier at roughly 41%. The newest chips are the binding reason: each B300 carries more high-bandwidth memory per chip than its predecessors, and HBM and DRAM fabrication capacity is being fought over against the phone and PC makers at Samsung, SK Hynix SKHY--, and Micron MU--. So the constraint has moved down the stack. A price list that shows memory inflating about twice as fast as the GPUs that consume it is a live reading that the bottleneck has shifted from GPU dies to the memory under them - information an investor can catch in a vendor notice before it shows up evenly across earnings.

...

Hold that, and the second half of the judgment follows. Nebius is a neocloud - a middleman that rents Nvidia hardware and passes the scarcity along. Its pricing power here is borrowed from upstream supply, not earned through a durable brand moat. That cuts two ways for the reader. On one side, the hike is useful even if you never own the stock: it is among the clearest real-time evidence available that AI compute demand is still running ahead of supply. On the other, pricing power under a shortage is not durable pricing power. Nebius is spending $20 billion to $25 billion on capital expenditures in 2026 and plans to build more than a gigawatt of new capacity a year by 2027 - the entire point of that buildout is to catch supply up to demand, which is exactly what eventually normalizes prices.
